Pinnacle
PIN-uh-kul
noun
From Latin pinnaculum, a little wing or peak, diminutive of pinna (a wing, point, or battlement); in the KJV it renders the Greek pterugion, a wing-like edge or summit, here the highest point of the temple.

Biblical Definition

A pinnacle is a wing-like summit or topmost point, the Greek pterugion, the highest edge of a building. In Scripture it names one exact place: the peak of the temple where Satan set the Lord Jesus in the second temptation. “Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple” (Mat 4:5); and Luke adds the tempter’s dare in full: “set him on a pinnacle of the temple, and said unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down from hence” (Luk 4:9). The devil quoted Scripture as he tempted — the promise that angels would bear Him up — urging Christ to fling Himself from the height and force a miracle of rescue. Our Lord answered with the deeper word: “Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah” (Deu 6:16). The pinnacle is therefore the very stage of presumption. To stand upon it and leap is not faith but the counterfeit of faith — demanding that God prove His care on our own reckless terms, twisting a true promise (Psa 91:11) into a pretext for tempting Him. Christ would not cast Himself down; He would be cast down in God’s time, at Calvary, in obedience and not in show. The pinnacle marks the height at which faith becomes presumption if it will not wait on God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A wing-like summit or highest point of a building; the peak of the temple in Christ’s temptation.

PINNACLE, noun. A turret, or part of a building elevated above the main structure; a high, spiring point; a summit.

In Scripture, the highest point of the temple, whither Satan carried Christ (Mat 4:5).

From Latin pinnaculum, a little wing or peak, from pinna, a wing or battlement.

Rendering the Greek pterugion, a wing-like edge or extremity.

Figuratively, the height at which trust in God may be perverted into the sin of tempting Him.

Key Scripture

Mat 4:5 — "Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple,"

Luk 4:9 — "And he brought him to Jerusalem, and set him on a pinnacle of the temple, and said unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down from hence:"

Deu 6:16 — "Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah."

Psa 91:11 — "For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways."

Modern Corruption

The pinnacle names a live corruption: presumption dressed as faith, the tempting of God by demanding He prove His care on our own terms.

expand to see more

On the pinnacle the devil dressed presumption as faith. He quoted a true promise — that angels would bear up the godly (Psa 91:11) — and urged Christ to prove it by a needless leap. This is a live and subtle corruption, for it wears the very language of trust. It says: if God loves me, let Him rescue me from the danger into which I have deliberately thrown myself; let Him work the miracle I demand, on the schedule I set, or His care is in doubt. Whole movements now teach believers to “name and claim,” to test God by casting themselves from spiritual heights and insisting He catch them. It is not faith. It is the sin of Massah.

Christ named it plainly: “Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God” (Deu 6:16). The corruption is answered not by doubting God’s promises but by refusing to abuse them. True faith trusts God in the way He appoints and does not manufacture crises to compel His hand. The angels do keep the godly in all their ways (Psa 91:11) — their ways, the paths of obedience, not the reckless leaps of self-will. Christ would not cast Himself from the pinnacle to make a show; He would go down to death in God’s time and God’s way. To recover the pinnacle is to see that demanding proof of God’s care on our own terms is not the height of faith but the counterfeit of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek pterugion, Latin pinnaculum — a wing-like summit, the peak of the temple.

expand to see more

Greek pterugion (G4419) — a wing-like edge or summit; the highest point of the temple

From Latin pinnaculum, diminutive of pinna (a wing, point, or battlement)

The place of Christ’s second temptation, where Satan bade Him cast Himself down (Mat 4:5; Luk 4:9)

The tempter misused a true promise (Psa 91:11) to urge a presumptuous leap

Answered by the law against tempting God: the sin of Massah (Deu 6:16)

Usage

"To leap from the pinnacle because a promise is written is not faith but the tempting of God."

"Satan quoted Scripture on the pinnacle — presumption often speaks the language of trust."

"Christ would not cast Himself down to make a show; He waited for the cross in God’s time."
